blocks.text: A prompt template is rarely finished the day it ships. Teams keep tweaking its wording as they learn what actually produces good output and what quietly confuses a model or a user.

The tricky part is that clients do not ask for a fresh copy of a prompt before every single use. A wording change on the server can sit invisible to a client that is still working from an older cached copy.
This lesson walks through why prompts drift over time, how a server signals that something changed, and how to keep an evolving prompt from breaking whoever is still calling it the old way.
1. Why a Prompt Template Wording Might Change
Teams rarely get a prompt exactly right on the first attempt. Real usage tends to reveal phrasing that reads as confusing, too blunt, or missing context the model actually needed.
A support team might notice their apology email prompt sounds too stiff. A legal team might ask for a disclaimer to be added to every response a prompt produces.
None of this is unusual. It is ordinary product iteration, and it happens to prompts exactly the way it happens to any other piece of user facing text.
2. What Actually Counts as a Change
A prompt can change in a few different ways, and they do not all carry the same risk. Wording changes, argument changes, and behavior changes each affect a client differently.
Wording changes are usually invisible to a client's code, since the argument names and count stay exactly the same. Argument changes are the ones that can actually break a request.
Behavior changes, where the same arguments now produce a meaningfully different kind of output, sit somewhere in between and deserve a clear description update either way.

blocks.text: 3. The Caching Problem: A Client Holding a Stale Copy

blocks.alt: A server updates a prompt while a client holds a stale cached copy

blocks.text: Most clients call prompts/list once, early in a session, and hold onto the result rather than asking again before every single use.
That cached copy is a snapshot in time. It stops matching reality the moment the server updates a prompt's wording, description, or argument list.
A client showing a stale argument list can ask a user for a field the server no longer expects, or fail to ask for one the server now requires.
4. Why Clients Cache Prompt Lists in the First Place
Caching prompts/list makes sense performance wise. Calling it again before every prompts/get would add a needless round trip for data that rarely changes.
The tradeoff is that a cache only stays useful as long as something tells it when the underlying data has actually changed.

blocks.title: A cache without a signal is just a guess
blocks.content: Without some kind of change notification, a client either refetches constantly, which wastes calls, or trusts a cache that might already be wrong, which is worse.

blocks.text: 5. The prompts/list_changed Notification

blocks.alt: A list changed notification tells the client to refresh its cache

blocks.text: MCP gives a server a direct way to solve this. It sends a notifications/prompts/list_changed message whenever the prompt list, or a specific prompt's definition, changes.
This is a notification, not a request. It carries no id and expects no reply, it simply tells the client that something changed.
6. What a Client Should Do When It Receives This Notification
On receiving the notification, a well behaved client should treat its current prompts/list cache as invalid right away.
It does not need to refetch mid keystroke, but it should schedule a fresh prompts/list call before serving anything from that cache again.

items: Mark the existing cached prompt list as stale as soon as the notification arrives.
Call prompts/list again before the next time a prompt is shown to a user or invoked.
Replace the cached copy entirely rather than trying to patch it in place.
Refresh any open form or menu that was already built from the old cached list.

blocks.title: Timing is a courtesy, not a guarantee
blocks.content: A client is free to refetch a moment later rather than instantly, but it should never keep serving a prompt definition it already knows is out of date.

8. Version Tagging Conventions in Prompt Names

blocks.alt: A prompt name can carry an explicit version tag

blocks.text: One common convention is baking a version number directly into a prompt's name, so summarize_ticket_v2 exists alongside the older summarize_ticket_v1.
This keeps both versions independently callable, which matters when some clients need real time to migrate to the newer one.
9. Version Tagging Inside the Description Instead
A lighter alternative is keeping one stable name and noting the version, and what changed, inside the description text instead.
This suits a change that only touches wording or tone, where every client that already knows the prompt's name can keep calling it unchanged.
10. Choosing Between Name Based and Description Based Versioning

blocks.alt: Name based versioning is compared against description based versioning

blocks.text: The right choice depends entirely on whether the change is safe for an unaware client to receive silently, or risky enough that it needs its own separate name.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Best suited for","What old clients see"],"rows":[["Name based, new prompt name per version","Argument changes, or any breaking change","The old name still works exactly as before"],["Description based, same name across versions","Wording or tone changes only","The same name, quietly improved behavior"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Backward Compatibility When Changing Arguments

blocks.alt: A backward compatible change keeps old callers working

blocks.text: Adding a brand new optional argument is safe. A client built before that argument existed simply never sends it, and the server falls back to a default.
Removing an argument, renaming one, or turning a previously optional argument into a required one, all break any client still calling the old way.

blocks.title: The safe direction only goes one way
blocks.content: It is always safe to add something optional. It is almost never safe to remove something, rename something, or tighten a requirement on something that already existed.

blocks.text: When a breaking change truly cannot wait, the fallback is giving the prompt a brand new name and letting the old one keep working exactly as clients expect.
12. Adding, Removing, and Renaming Arguments Compared

blocks.alt: Adding an argument, removing one, and renaming one carry different risk

blocks.text: It helps to lay out the common kinds of argument edits side by side, since they carry very different levels of risk.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Argument change","Safe for existing clients"],"rows":[["Add a new optional argument","Yes, old clients are unaffected"],["Add a new required argument","No, old clients omit it and the call fails"],["Remove an existing argument","No, some clients still send it, though most servers can just ignore an unexpected field"],["Rename an existing argument","No, functionally the same as removing the old one"],["Change optional to required","No, old clients that used to omit it now fail"]]}

blocks.text: 13. Deprecating an Old Prompt Version Gracefully

blocks.alt: An old prompt version is deprecated gracefully alongside the new one

blocks.text: When a breaking change is genuinely needed, the kindest path is keeping the old version alive for a while rather than deleting it the moment the new one ships.

items: Keep the old prompt name listed, but mark it deprecated in its own description text.
State a rough date or milestone by which the old version will be removed.
Ship the new version alongside it under its own name, not as a silent replacement.
Watch actual usage of the old version before finally removing it from the list.

blocks.text: 14. Coordinating Server Restarts and Notification Timing
A server should send notifications/prompts/list_changed at the moment its prompt definitions actually change, not only on a fresh restart.

If a deploy changes prompt wording, the notification belongs right after that new version becomes live, so a connected client's cache goes stale at the correct moment rather than staying stale indefinitely.
15. Testing a Prompt Template After a Change
Before shipping any prompt edit, it is worth calling prompts/get with the same arguments the old version used, and reading the filled messages closely.
Look for anything the new wording accidentally broke, a placeholder left unfilled, a sentence that no longer makes sense, or a tone that drifted further than intended.

code.content:
# Manual test checklist after editing a prompt template
# 1. Call prompts/get with a known good set of arguments from before the change
# 2. Read the filled messages fully, do not just skim the first line
# 3. Confirm every placeholder still resolves and nothing reads as empty or broken
# 4. Confirm the tone and length still fit the prompt's stated purpose
# 5. If arguments changed at all, test with old style calls too, to see how they now behave

blocks.text: 16. Documenting Changes for Consumers
A short changelog note attached to a prompt, whether in its description or in separate docs, saves every team relying on it from having to guess what shifted.
Stating the date, what changed, and whether the change is safe for an existing client to receive silently turns a surprise into a routine update.

items: A plain language summary of what changed, wording, arguments, or behavior.
Whether existing clients need to do anything at all.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Consider draft_apology_email, currently at description v2, with two required arguments, customer_name and issue_description.
The team wants to add a refund_offered field, and separately wants to soften the tone of the generated email.

Since the tone change and the new argument are both non breaking, description based versioning is enough here. No new prompt name is needed, and a list_changed notification tells every connected client to pick up the update.
Common Mistakes

items: Changing a required argument or removing one without giving the prompt a new name.
Editing a prompt's wording on the server without ever sending notifications/prompts/list_changed.
Assuming a client will refetch prompts/list on its own schedule instead of reacting to the notification.
Deleting an old prompt version the same day a new one ships, with no warning period.
Skipping a fresh round of testing after a wording edit because the arguments did not change.
Leaving a changelog entirely out of a prompt's description, so nobody can tell what shifted or when.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the summarize_ticket prompt, currently at v1 with a single required argument, ticket_text.
Write the v2 name based entry that adds a new optional priority_hint argument, and write the list_changed notification a server would send right after deploying it.
Key Takeaway
Prompt wording naturally drifts as teams learn what works, and a client's cached copy drifts along with it until something tells the client to refresh.

The list_changed notification is that signal, version tags in a name or description communicate what shifted, and testing after every change keeps a drifting prompt from quietly breaking whoever still relies on it.
